svg.title: Why traffic engineering exists: the cost of IGP shortest path, what TE buys, and what it costs
svg.desc: Upper left: a topology with two paths between the same pair, one at 10 Gbps and one at 1 Gbps, and the note that the IGP sends both flows down the shorter path until it saturates while the other link stays idle. Upper right: the four capabilities TE adds, CSPF path computation from a traffic-engineering database, bandwidth reservation, fast reroute with pre-computed backup, and automatic bandwidth adjustment. Lower left: the four costs of TE, state on every router along the path, a second control plane to operate, tunnels that must be re-optimised, and complex failure behaviour. Lower right: the three current alternatives, segment routing which removes per-flow state, SD-WAN which moves the decision to an application policy layer, and over-provisioning which is cheaper until it is not. A closing band gives the deciding question.
svg.text: Traffic engineering exists because shortest path is not the same as least loaded
Four capabilities, four costs, and three alternatives that did not exist when TE was invented
The problem
PE-A
PE-B
short path · 1G · saturated
longer path · 10G · idle
The IGP compares costs, not occupancy, so it fills the small link first and
What TE adds
1. CSPF: path chosen from the TE database, not from hop cost.
2. Reservation: the bandwidth is promised, not hoped for.
3. Fast reroute: a backup path exists before the failure.
4. Automatic bandwidth: tunnels resize as traffic shifts.
Only 2 is genuinely new; 1, 3 and 4 can be done without RSVP.
What it costs
State on every router along every tunnel, which grows with
tunnels rather than with sites.
A second control plane to operate, with its own timers.
Re-optimisation as a scheduled task nobody owns.
Failure behaviour that is harder to explain than routing.
The three alternatives now available
Segment routing: source-routed paths, no per-flow state.
SD-WAN: policy per application, measured per path.
Over-provisioning: buy bandwidth instead of engineering it.
All three are cheaper to operate than RSVP-TE at most scales.
None of them gives a hard bandwidth guarantee per flow.
The deciding question: do you need a per-flow bandwidth guarantee that the network enforces, or do you need traffic to avoid a congested link?
The first is TE and only TE does it. The second is a routing preference, and segment routing or a metric change solves it with a fraction of the state.
Most RSVP-TE deployments were bought for the second reason and are now maintained for the first, which is why they outlive their justification.
